headline: High-risk filesystem and shell overlap: xonsh can read/write and egress broadly while mem0 may ingest trusted content, creating prompt-injection, leakage, and cascading-error pathways.

A_prompt_injection.rationale: mem0 has no shared channel documented, but xonsh exposes stdin/stdout, filesystem, and shell execution, so if its outputs are copied into mem0 or a shared workspace, mem0 could treat attacker-controlled content as trusted memory. The pairwise pathway is inferred, not directly evidenced.
conditions: IF xonsh output is copied into mem0 prompts or memory records
IF both agents share a writable workspace or files are manually transferred between them
mitigations: Restrict mem0 ingestion to allowlisted sources only
Separate workspaces for the two agents
Add a human review step before mem0 stores xonsh-generated text
Strip instructions from xonsh outputs before ingestion
requires-engineering: add provenance tagging for transferred content

B_data_leakage.rationale: xonsh can read filesystem contents and has broad network egress, while mem0 is a knowledge-management agent with no network egress documented. If sensitive files are present in a shared workspace, xonsh can expose them through its outputs or downstream network calls; mem0 may then persist or surface them. The interaction is plausible but not directly documented.
conditions: IF sensitive files are accessible in the same filesystem namespace
IF xonsh forwards file contents or derived text to external services
mitigations: Remove sensitive files from any shared directory
Disable or proxy xonsh network egress for sensitive sessions
Use separate OS users for each agent
Review xonsh commands before execution on sensitive data
requires-engineering: enforce per-agent data-loss-prevention controls

C_capability_conflict.rationale: xonsh can write the filesystem and spawn subprocesses, while mem0 is a knowledge-management system with no write surface documented. If both operate on the same directory, concurrent writes or state changes can conflict even without git modification. The conflict is real but narrower than high because no shared locking or git state is shown.
conditions: IF both agents write to the same directory
IF mem0 persists memory artifacts into files that xonsh also edits
mitigations: Assign disjoint output directories
Serialize writes with a simple operator checklist
Back up shared files before runs
Use read-only mounts for one agent
requires-engineering: add file-locking around shared artifacts

D_cascading_error.rationale: xonsh can generate shell output and act on it, while mem0 can store or retrieve that content as memory. If mem0 treats xonsh-produced text as authoritative, errors can cascade from one agent into later actions or summaries. Because no verification workflow is documented, uncertainty pushes this to medium.
conditions: IF mem0 stores xonsh output without verification
IF later xonsh commands are generated from mem0-retrieved text
mitigations: Require source citations for stored facts
Add a verification step before reuse
Mark xonsh output as untrusted by default
Limit mem0 retention for command-derived notes
requires-engineering: implement provenance-aware retrieval

E_compliance.rationale: No specific residency, certification, or retention mismatch is documented for mem0 or xonsh, and neither profile lists regulated data classes. The only concrete compliance concern is that xonsh touches filesystem contents and environment variables, so operator handling could create policy gaps, but the pair itself is not shown to violate a regime.
conditions: IF regulated data is placed in xonsh-accessible files
IF mem0 retention settings differ from the operator's policy
mitigations: Avoid placing regulated data in shared files
Document retention expectations before use
Review environment variables for secrets
Use separate storage for regulated workloads
requires-engineering: map data flows to compliance controls
